label: short_circuit
graph_version: 3.9.8 (3.9.7 + one primary per misconception (S9c) and the four remaining sibling edges (S9b), 2026-11-04; listed in revision_3_9_8)

edges.label:
[0] everyday_reading (E): Folk meaning: in maths and logic the value of 'p and q' is read off a truth table with both sides known, so both sides are always 'computed'. Java rule: && and || evaluate left to right and skip the right operand when the left already decides the result (false && x, true || x).
[1] misconception (M) -> NoShortCircuit: wrong rule: Logical AND/OR always evaluate both sides. Right rule: In p && q, q is evaluated only when p is true; in p || q, q is evaluated only when p is false.
[2] misconception (M) -> SingleAmpersandForAnd: wrong rule: & and | are the same as && and || for conditions, so either can be used. Right rule: && and || skip the right operand when the left decides the result; & and | always evaluate both, which fails when the right side depends on the left (e.g. x != 0 & y / x > 1).
[3] inconsistent_trace (T) -> NoShortCircuit: Points to LT (evaluate the left operand; stop if it decides; otherwise evaluate the right). Applied unevenly: on some passes of a loop the student counts the side effect of the right operand (e.g. ++i) although the left operand was already false, or lets a guarded index be read on the pass where the guard failed. (here mixing in: "logical AND/OR always evaluate both sides (Java short-circuits them)")

[0] names_the_element (N): Short-circuit evaluation is the way Java evaluates the logical operators && and ||: the second operand is evaluated only if necessary.
[1] states_the_rule (S): In a && b, b is evaluated only if a is true (false && b is false); in a || b, b is evaluated only if a is false (true || b is true). &, | and ^ do not short-circuit.

[0] line_by_line_trace (LT): Evaluate the left operand fully; if it is false (for &&) or true (for ||) the whole expression takes that value immediately; otherwise evaluate the right operand, whose value is the result.
[1] output_prediction (OP): The value is the same as under full evaluation whenever the right operand would have completed normally; with n = 0, (n != 0 && 10 / n > 1) is false and throws no exception.
[2] one_step_execution (OS): When the right operand is skipped, none of its side effects happen: with i = 0, after (false && ++i > 0) i is still 0, while (true && ++i > 0) makes i 1.

[0] relation_to_neighbour (R): Short-circuiting is the defining evaluation order of && and || only; the book's other boolean operators (! and ^, and & / | if used) evaluate all their operands.
[1] purpose_of_the_whole (P): Guard plan: put the safety test first so the risky test runs only when it is safe, e.g. (i < a.length && a[i] != 0), (count != 0 && sum / count > 5), (str == null || str.isEmpty()).

[0] predict_a_change (C) -> NoShortCircuit: Swapping the operands of a guard (a[i] != 0 && i < a.length) keeps the truth table but lets the risky test run first and throw; replacing && by & removes the protection; moving a needed side effect into the right operand makes it happen only sometimes.
[1] transfer_to_a_new_program (X): Rely on short-circuiting when the second test is only valid or meaningful if the first holds (bounds, zero, null) or is expensive; do not put side effects you need into the right operand.
[2] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: The protecting test must be the left operand of && / ||. Kind: run-time exception. Trigger class: A guard written after the test it protects, or with & / |: index out of bounds, divisor 0, or null when the guard condition is false.
[3] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: The right operand of && / || is not always evaluated. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: A required side effect (++, assignment, method call) placed in the right operand, on runs where the left operand decides the result.
